rv.q: The superb Lauren Ambrose plays her like a woman at sea, frantically swimming — exhausted, disoriented, barely afloat but undeterred.

The play's almost clinical approach to the investigation and its impact on the family has an admirable forensic authenticity, but Miriam's anguish is left so little explored that her plight never becomes particularly affecting or illuminating.
Their lack of depth makes it hard for The Unbelievers to sustain our belief.
The Unbelievers is a moving, haunting, and theatrical dramatization of a traumatic real life issue.
And with Ambrose as the lead, it's unmissable.

Far from your typical family drama about grief, The Unbelievers is a knotty, elusive, thought-provoking play that keeps you on your toes, utilizes constantly shifting timelines and tones to great effect, and leaves audiences with a lot to unpack, and admire, once they leave the theatre.
If you’re not sobbing (openly or silently) – whether you’re a parent or not – as these words are spoken by Ambrose, perhaps you aren’t alive.

Lauren Ambrose, best known for her film and television work but also a veteran of several Broadway productions, is a knockout in the part, fearlessly summoning not only this mother’s grief and rage but the flashes of confusion and pettiness that arise as she grapples with unimaginable trauma.
But it can be trying and somehow unnecessarily contrived.
Ultimately, however, the main problem with The Unbelievers is one of belief: The characters generally act not organically but according to the playwright's whim.
This small, seemingly inconsequential scene of eating and talking is breathtaking in context, and a wave of calm washes over both the actors and the audience as Miriam’s world begins to right itself.
Lauren Ambrose answers with a performance so ferocious that the waiting itself becomes the drama.

While The Unbelievers proves unconvincing as a domestic drama, it offers a riveting character study of a woman who responds to an unthinkable situation in the only way she knows how, all others be damned.
Lauren Ambrose’s riveting lead performance can’t fully elevate a show that doesn’t quite go deep enough.

cn.t: Ambrose delivers a devastating, tour-de-force performance as a mother grappling with her son's disappearance, but Payne's emotionally detached, time-shifting drama divides critics on whether it goes deep enough into its harrowing subject matter.

vr.q: The Unbelievers had me mostly on the edge of my seat with its compelling premise and even more compelling ensemble work.
